content: Jet lag, also referred to as jetlag or jet-lag, is a physiological condition that arises due to disruptions in the body’s circadian rhythm. These disruptions can occur as a result of shift work, changes in daylight saving time, variations in day length, or, as the name suggests, transmeridian travel, such as flying across multiple time zones on a jet plane. This condition is also known by terms such as desynchronosis, dysrhythmia, dyschrony, or jet syndrome. The primary cause of jet lag is believed to be the disturbance of the light/dark cycle, which regulates the body’s circadian rhythm. Environmental factors can further exacerbate this condition. Jet lag symptoms can persist for several days, and medical experts generally estimate a recovery rate of approximately one day per time zone crossed. Adopting good sleep hygiene can facilitate faster recovery from jet lag. Practices such as adequate sleep, relaxation, moderate exercise, and a balanced diet are considered effective methods for recovery. However, the experience of jet lag varies significantly among individuals, making it challenging to determine the efficacy of any single remedy. Age may influence the severity of jet lag, with younger individuals often experiencing more pronounced symptoms compared to older adults. Women may also be more susceptible to jet lag than men, partly due to the sensitivity of estrogen to jet lag-like conditions. A recent study conducted on hamsters demonstrated that sildenafil (commercially known as Viagra) accelerated recovery from circadian rhythm shifts comparable to eastward travel in humans by 50%, even at low doses. However, this application has not been tested in humans and is considered an off-label use by the drug’s manufacturers. When traveling across multiple time zones, the body’s internal clock becomes misaligned with the local time at the destination. This misalignment occurs because the body experiences daylight and darkness at times that conflict with its accustomed rhythms. The body’s natural patterns, which regulate eating, sleeping, hormone secretion, and body temperature, are disrupted and may no longer correspond to the external environment or to each other. The term jet lag describes the physical symptoms that arise because the body cannot immediately realign these rhythms. The rate at which the body adjusts to new daylight and darkness hours varies among individuals. While some people may take several days to adapt to a new time zone, others experience minimal disruption to their natural patterns. It is uncommon to experience jet lag when crossing only one or two time zones. There have been suggestions that jet lag may be linked to cabin air contamination by tricresyl phosphate (TCP) from engine bleed air, which supplies the cabin pressurization system. However, these claims have not been substantiated, and aircraft manufacturers maintain that cabin air quality is generally high. The symptoms of jet lag can vary widely but often include the following: Dehydration, potentially due to the dry air on airplanes. Loss of appetite. Nausea or an upset stomach. Headaches or sinus irritation. Fatigue. Disorientation or grogginess. Insomnia or highly irregular sleep patterns. Irritability or irrational behavior. Mild depression. Frequent time zone changes, long working hours, or rotating shifts can lead to reduced productivity, alertness, and safety, with an estimated economic cost of $70 billion annually. The severity of jet lag is influenced more by the number of time zones crossed (east-west) than by the distance traveled. For example, a ten-hour flight from Frankfurt to Johannesburg (traveling south, staying on the same meridian) is less likely to induce jet lag than a five-hour flight between New York and Los Angeles (crossing time zones). The International Date Line does not directly contribute to jet lag, as the maximum possible disruption is plus or minus 12 hours. If the time difference between two locations exceeds 12 hours, the difference should be subtracted from 24 to calculate the effective time disruption. For instance, a 20-hour time difference equates to 4 hours of jet lag. Layovers can complicate this calculation. Jet lag can be particularly challenging near the North and South Poles, where extreme periods of daylight or darkness occur depending on the time of year. These conditions often lead to insomnia or hypersomnia. There is evidence suggesting that traveling eastward is more disruptive than traveling westward. This may be because eastward flights counteract the body’s natural circadian rhythm. Most individuals have a circadian period slightly longer than 24 hours, making it easier to stay up later than to wake up earlier. Additionally, eastward flights are more likely to require individuals to stay awake for more than one full night to adjust to the local time zone. For example, consider the following scenarios: A westward flight from London to Los Angeles involves an 8-hour time zone difference. This is equivalent to staying up all night and going to bed at 6 a.m. the next day, 8 hours later than usual. An eastward flight from Los Angeles to London involves the same time zone difference but is equivalent to staying up all night and going to bed at 2 p.m. the next day, 16 hours later than usual. People who rely on updated information from other time zones may experience biological clock variations, making it harder to align with the social routines of their geographical surroundings. This phenomenon, sometimes referred to as net lag, can result in symptoms similar to jet lag during the adaptation period.
